newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich using Dole loan to pay $300,000 penalty.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich using Dole loan to pay $300,000 penalty.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich announced on Thursday he will pay a $300,000 ethics penalty with a loan from 1996 Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole.

Gingrich's effort to escape a political dilemma -- how to pay a heavy penalty from personal resources as critics demand -- produced the unique and unexpected prospect of one American political celebrity riding to the rescue of another.
It was an outcome that enraged some Democrats, generally pleased Republicans and surprised political Washington.

Gingrich, struggling to get a nagging controversy behind him and recover lost political clout, announced he would pay the $300,000 penalty levied by House vote in January with a loan from Dole, the retired former Senate majority leader and losing 1996 presidential candidate.
A press summary said it would be a legal obligation and would carry a 10 percent interest rate compounded annually.

The idea was to give Gingrich a way to pay off a heavy debt without using campaign donations or other publicly donated funds -- and his camp said the offer of this solution came from Dole, a man who has amassed some private wealth.
"This was Dole's overture. This was something Dole wanted to do. It was his inititiave," said Gingrich's Press Secretary Christina Martin.
The loan would be due and payable within eight years, collectible only from Gingrich and could not be forgiven, the statement said.
It said Gingrich could have used campaign funds or a trust fund to pay the penalty but the speaker said he had a moral obligation to use his personal funds.
"Marianne (his wife) and I decided, whatever the consequences, we had to do what was best, what was right, morally and spiritually," Gingrich said.
A separate statement by Dole applauded Gingrich's decision, saying the speaker had "yet again shown himself to be a man of integrity" and had set an example of accountability and ethics.
"For that reason and many more, Newt is a friend and I am pleased that I can be of assistance," Dole said.
"I consider this not only an opportunity to help a friend but a long-term investment in the party," he said.

Dole was beaten handily by Democratic President Bill Clinton last November but has remained in the public eye, often appearing in television commercials and flashing a relaxed, self-deprecating wit on talk shows.
The penalty, which Gingrich maintains should not be called a fine, was assessed by the House ethics committee to meet some of the costs of its two-year investigation of Gingrich.

It was approved by the House when it voted to 395-28 to reprimand Gingrich in January for using tax-exempt funds to promote political goals and misleading House investigators. He was the first speaker ever to be so reprimanded by his Congressional colleagues.
Although the press statement said Gingrich's action "puts this matter to rest," Democrats quickly assailed the arrangement in floor speeches.

Representative George Miller, a California Democrat, charged that Dole was a "lobbyist" for the tobacco industry during last year's presidential campaign when Dole questioned whether tobacco was addictive.
"This is a sad day for the House of Representatives when the tobacco industry is paying the legal fines," Miller said.

Similarly, Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut said Gingrich "brought discredit upon the House. He admitted he lied to the Congress. Republicans are celebrating the fact that Newt Gingrich is paying a $300,000 for lying to Congress."
But Gingrich found an important sympathiser in Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle, who said he saw nothing improper in Gingrich's acceptance of a loan from Dole.
"I've got a call in to Bob Dole for a loan myself," Daschle quipped. "I think Speaker Gingrich handled this matter by and large in a manner most people will find reasonably acceptable.
Republican Tillie Fowler of Florida said, as did other Gingrich loyalists, that "I commend the speaker" for reimbursing the ethics committee out of his own money.

Gingrich's lawyer Randy Evans told reporters it was decided not to get a loan from a bank or commercial institution because they might have legislation affecting them before Congress, raising conflict-of-interest concerns.
"His intention is not to pay this back from gifts," Evans said.
